L74: Horiuchi, Horiuchi, and Mizuno (1, 2) made the striking
L75: 
L76: observation that when inorganic phosphate became limiting in
L77: 
L78: the growth medium of certain strains of Escherichia coli, there
L79: 
L80: resulted a high level of alkaline phosphatase activity. The same
L81: 
L82: discovery was made independently by Torriani (3). Recently,
L83: 
L84: other strains of
L85: 
L86: E.
L87: 
L88: coli have been found in which formation of
L89: 
L90: alkaline phosphatase occurs in the presence of inorganic ortho-
L91: 
L92: phosphate (4), and these provide a more convenient source of
L93: material for fractionation. Garen and Levinthal (5) purified the
L94: 
L95: enzyme and studied some of its properties. Purification proce-
L96: 
L97: dures were also developed by Plocke and Vallee,’ and by Schwartz
L98: 
L99: and Lipmann.’
L100: 
L101: We became interested in this enzyme as a possible reagent
L102: 
L103: for the removal of terminal, monoesterified phosphate from poly-
L104: 
L105: nucleotides because preparations of human semen phosphatase
L106: 
L107: and other monophosphatases tried in this laboratory have not
L108: been satisfactory for this purpose. Some months ago, Drs.
L109: 
L110: Garen and Levinthal gave us a number of samples of this alkaline
L111: 
L112: phosphatase and under the conditions initially studied, we found
L113: 
L114: it to be suit.able for removal of terminal, monoesterified phos-
L115: 
L116: phate from a variety of ribo-oligonucleotides. Successful results
L117: 
L118: have also been obtained with deoxyribo-oligonucleotides (6).
L119: 
L120: However, we encountered difficulties in treating “soluble ribo-
L121: nucleic acid” with this phosphatase. High levels of enzyme and
L122: 
L123: prolonged periods of incubation were required, and under these
L124: 
L125: conditions we could indeed detect the cleaving of phosphodiester
L126: 
L127: bonds. The relation of the ribonuclease and phosphomono-
L128: 
L129: esterase activities in
L130: 
L131: E.
L132: 
L133: coli alkaline phosphatase preparations
L134: 
L135: will be examined in a future publication.2
L136: 
L137: This paper will report certain observations on substrate speci-
L138: 
L139: ficity and other properties of
L140: 
L141: E.
L142: 
L143: co& alkaline phosphatase. The
L144: enzyme hydrolyzes a wide variety of compounds containing
L145: 
L146: monosubstituted phosphate, including adenosine triphosphate
L147: 
L148: and other nucleoside polyphosphates, PPi, PPPi, and short-
L149: 
L150: chain polymetaphosphates. A number of experiments were
L151: 
L152: done to show that AMP, PPi, and ATP are indeed hydrolyzed
L153: 
L154: by the same enzyme, because of earlier reports that PPi and
L155: 
L156: ATP are not cleaved by the
L157: 
L158: E.
L159: 
L160: coli phosphatase (3, 5). Several
L161: 
L162: unusual properties were encountered, such as slowly reversible
L163: heat inactivation, a remarkable similarity in the Michaelis con-
L164: 
L165: stants and maximal velocity constants for a wide variety of
L166: 
L167: phosphate esters, and a biphasic curve relating substrate concen-
L168: 
L169: tration and activity.

L1452: DISCUSSION
L1453: 
L1454: To an unusual degree, the alkaline phosphatase of
L1455: 
L1456: E. coli
L1457: 
L1458: appears to interact specifically with monosubstituted phosphate,
L1459: 
L1460: and other structural features of the substrate molecule seem to
L1461: 
L1462: play a relatively minor role. This is indicated by the remarkable
L1463: 
L1464: similarities in
L1465: 
L1466: V,,,
L1467: 
L1468: and
L1469: 
L1470: K,

L1473: strong competitive inhibition by Pi previously noted (2,5). The
L1474: 
L1475: inhibition by Pi is a practical disadvantage because it becomes
L1476: 
L1477: necessary to use relatively large amounts of enzyme to secure
L1478: 
L1479: essential completion of the reaction. In spite of this, the enzyme
L1480: 
L1481: can be safely used as an enzymic reagent to remove terminal
L1482: 
L1483: phosphate from ribo-oligonucleotides. However, caution must
L1484: 
L1485: be exercised, for ribonuclease activity can be detected, especially
L1486: 
L1487: with large ribopolynucleotides.

L1490: E.
L1491: 
L1492: coli alkaline phosphatase
L1493: 
L1494: hydrolyzes nucleoside polyphosphates, PPi, PPPi, and short
L1495: 
L1496: chain metaphosphates. A number of enzymes that produce Pi
L1497: 
L1498: from relatively low molecular weight metaphosphate have been
L1499: 
L1500: described (34,35), but these appear also to cleave phosphodiester
L1501: 
L1502: bonds in cyclic trimetaphosphate at comparable rates. As
L1503: 
L1504: expected from the uniformity in values of
L1505: 
L1506: K,
L1507: 
L1508: and
L1509: 
L1510: V,,,,

L1513:

L1515: initial phase of reaction when an equimolar mixture is incubated
L1516: 
L1517: with the phosphatase. On the other hand, partial hydrolysis
L1518: 
L1519: of ATP results in accumulation of AMP and some ADP, with
L1520: 
L1521: very little formation of adenosine. This results from the fact
L1522: 
L1523: that Pi is a strong competitive inhibitor for the hydrolysis of

L1527: As mentioned above, it was reported earlier that PPi and ATP
L1528: 
L1529: are not hydrolyzed by this enzyme (3, 5). We have had several
L1530: discussions with Drs. Torriani and Levinthal, but it is still not
L1531: 
L1532: clear why they did not observe cleaving of ATP and PPi. Pre-

L1534: sumably an inhibitor was present in their incubation mixtures.

L1536: If the hydrolysis of pyrophosphate esters could be suppressed in
